sources.text: --- title: Eisenstein and Mellin Formulas for Quaternionic Elliptic Coefficients description: Eisenstein and harmonic-theta formulas for convergent quaternionic elliptic coefficients, including an explicit cubic-lattice critical value. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: research order: 7 --- # Eisenstein and Mellin Formulas for Quaternionic Elliptic Coefficients :::discussion Varying a four-dimensional lattice turns the elliptic coefficients into automorphic functions on a special linear group. We identify both their inducing data and the irreducible module they generate. This is a different group action from the Möbius action on the ball. ::: ## Harmonic numerators of the kernel derivatives ::::lemma EI1 | Harmonic numerators in every derivative order Version: 1 Uses: [Kernel](foundations.md#f-d3), [multi-indices](directions.md#n-d1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $\nu\in\mathbb N_0^3$, $r=|\nu|$, and $N(q)=|q|^2$, there is a quaternion-valued homogeneous polynomial $H_\nu$ of degree $r+1$, with harmonic real components, such that $$ G_\nu(q)=\frac{H_\nu(q)}{N(q)^{r+2}}. $$ It obeys $H_0=\bar q$ and $H_{\nu+e_j}=N\partial_jH_\nu-2(r+2)x_jH_\nu$. :::proof Proof of EI1 Start with $H_0=\bar q$. Differentiation gives the recurrence $$ H_{\nu+e_j}=N\partial_jH_\nu-2(r+2)x_jH_\nu. \tag{E3} $$ It is polynomial and has degree $r+2$. If $H_\nu$ is harmonic of degree $r+1$, then $$ \Delta(N\partial_jH_\nu)=(4r+8)\partial_jH_\nu, \qquad \Delta(x_jH_\nu)=2\partial_jH_\nu, $$ so (E3) is harmonic. This proves the lemma for every order. ::: :::: :::discussion The lattice sums $E_\nu(L)$ and their relation to derivatives of the regular part of $\wp_{L,j}$ are established in [N1–N3](directions.md#n1). They converge for $r>1$, and even $r$ gives zero. We therefore focus on odd $r\ge3$. Ordinary Taylor coefficients include the multi-index factorials. ::: ## Homogeneous sections and Eisenstein summation Set $G_4=\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb R)$, $\Gamma=\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb Z)$, and $K_4=\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Vectors act on the right, and $L_g=\mathbb Z^4g$. For real $w>4$, write $I_w$ for the space of smooth functions $f:\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C$ such that $$ f(tx)=|t|^{-w}f(x)\qquad(x\ne0,\ t\in\mathbb R^\times). $$ The condition with $t=-1$ makes every $f\in I_w$ even. The action of $G_4$ is $$ (R(g)f)(x)=f(xg). $$ Homogeneity is preserved because $(tx)g=t(xg)$, and $R(g)R(h)=R(gh)$ follows from $(xg)h=x(gh)$. ::::construction EI-C1 | The lattice Eisenstein function Version: 1 Uses: [homogeneous-function model](#ei-d1). Justification: Convergence, smoothness, and equivariance in [EI2](#ei2). Origin: derivation --- For $w>4$ and $f\in I_w$, form $$ \mathcal E_f(g)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^4\setminus\{0\}}f(mg). $$ :::: Let $e_4=(0,0,0,1)$ and $$ P=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}:\det(A)d=1\right\}, \qquad F_f(g)=f(e_4g). $$ The primitive-vector regrouping in EI2 specializes, for a radial section, to the [Epstein–Eisenstein identity](lattice-eisenstein-background.md#ei-b1) [[7, Lemma 2.9]](#ref-sands-2022). ::::theorem EI2 | A maximal-parabolic Eisenstein series Version: 1 Uses: [homogeneous-function model](#ei-d1), [EI-C1](#ei-c1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $w>4$, $\mathcal E_f$ is smooth, left $\Gamma$-invariant, of moderate growth with all right derivatives, and satisfies $\mathcal E_{R(h)f}(g)=\mathcal E_f(gh)$. Moreover $$ \mathcal E_f(g)=2\zeta(w)\sum_{\gamma\in(P\cap\Gamma)\backslash\Gamma}F_f(\gamma g). $$ The section law is $F_f(pg)=|d|^{-w}F_f(g)$. In normalized left-equivariant/right-translation induction, with $\delta_P(p)=|d|^{-4}$, the inducing character is $\chi(p)=|d|^{2-w}$. For an odd derivative order $r\ge3$, the scalar components of $G_\nu$ give $w=r+3$ and $\chi=|d|^{-(r+1)}$. :::proof Proof of EI2 The sum and all its $g$-derivatives converge uniformly on compact subsets of $G_4$: differentiation preserves degree $-w$, and $|mg|\gg_C|m|$ on a compact set $C$. Hence $\mathcal E_f$ is smooth, left $\Gamma$-invariant, and $$ \mathcal E_{R(h)f}(g)=\mathcal E_f(gh). \tag{E6} $$ Each scalar component of $G_\nu$ is such an $f$, so EI-C1 includes the original coefficient sums. The bound $|\mathcal E_f(g)|\le C_f\|g^{-1}\|^w\sum_{m\ne0}|m|^{-w}$, and the same bound for right derivatives, gives moderate growth. Let $P$ be the maximal parabolic consisting of matrices $$ p=\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det(A)d=1, $$ which stabilizes the row line $\mathbb R e_4$. Put $F_f(g)=f(e_4g)$. Then $$ F_f(pg)=|d|^{-w}F_f(g),\qquad \delta_P(p)=|d|^{-4}. \tag{E7} $$ Every primitive integral row occurs as $e_4\gamma$, and the stabilizer of the primitive line is $P\cap\Gamma$. Grouping a nonzero row by its positive gcd and then identifying opposite primitive rows gives $$ \boxed{\mathcal E_f(g)=2\zeta(w) \sum_{\gamma\in(P\cap\Gamma)\backslash\Gamma}F_f(\gamma g).} \tag{E8} $$ This is a maximal-parabolic Eisenstein series in its region of absolute convergence. In the left-equivariant/right-translation convention $F(pg)=\delta_P(p)^{1/2}\chi(p)F(g)$, its **normalized inducing character** is $$ \chi(p)=|d|^{2-w}=|d|^{-(r+1)}. \tag{E9} $$ Specifying the section law removes any ambiguity from authors who use the inverse character or opposite parabolic. ::: :::: ## The irreducible module selected by the coefficients For even $w\ge6$ put $d=w-4$, and let $\mathcal P_d$ be the homogeneous degree-$d$ polynomials on $\mathbb R^4$, with action $p(x)\mapsto p(xg)$. Let $d\sigma$ be Euclidean surface measure on $S^3$. ::::definition EI-D2 | The Vanishing-Moment Subspace Version: 1 Uses: [homogeneous-function model](#ei-d1). --- For even $w\ge6$, the **vanishing-moment subspace** of $I_w$ is $$ \mathcal M_w=\left\{f\in I_w:\int_{S^3}f(\omega)p(\omega)d\sigma(\omega)=0 \text{ for every }p\in\mathcal P_d\right\}. \tag{E10} $$ :::: Write $\mathcal Y_l$ for complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ restricted to $S^3$; $V_l=\operatorname{Sym}^l\mathbb C^2$. ::::proposition EI3 | Moment kernel and finite-dimensional quotient Version: 1 Uses: [EI-D2](#ei-d2), [EI1](#ei1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For even $w\ge6$, the moment map gives an equivariant exact sequence $$ 0\to\mathcal M_w\to I_w\to\mathcal P_{w-4}^{\vee}\to0. $$ Its compact-finite kernel is $\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathcal Y_{w-2+2j}$. Every scalar derivative kernel of order $r=w-3$ lies in its minimal compact type $\mathcal Y_{w-2}$. :::proof Proof of EI3 The pairing is bilinear, not Hermitian. Since the product has degree $-4$, angular change of variables under $g\in\mathrm{SL}_4$ shows $$ \int_{S^3}f(\omega g)p(\omega g)d\sigma(\omega) =\int_{S^3}f(\omega)p(\omega)d\sigma(\omega). $$ Indeed for $\eta=\omega g/|\omega g|$, $d\sigma(\eta)=|\omega g|^{-4}d\sigma(\omega)$. Thus (E10) is invariant, and the pairing induces an exact sequence $$ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal M_w\longrightarrow I_w \longrightarrow\mathcal P_{w-4}^{\vee}\longrightarrow0. \tag{E11} $$ Surjectivity follows from the nondegenerate spherical pairing on the finite-dimensional polynomial space. Harmonic decomposition of $\mathcal P_{w-4}$ gives $$ (\mathcal M_w)_{K_4}=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathcal Y_{w-2+2j}, \tag{E12} $$ where the subscript means $K_4$-finite vectors. The low harmonics $\mathcal Y_0,\mathcal Y_2,\ldots,\mathcal Y_{w-4}$ constitute the finite-dimensional quotient. By EI1, every scalar Fueter kernel derivative of order $r=w-3$ belongs to the **minimal compact type** $\mathcal Y_{w-2}$ of this kernel. ::: :::: For the general real degenerate principal series, see [[4, Thms. 1.1–1.2]](#ref-gourevitch-2017). With normalized $P_{3,1}$ induction, the restriction of $|\det|^{w-2}\times1$ to $\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb R)$ has the section law $|d|^{-w}$. EI4 gives the harmonic-transition argument for this restriction. ::::theorem EI4 | Irreducibility and harmonic transitions Version: 1 Uses: [EI3](#ei3), irreducibility of spherical harmonics under $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- The $(\mathfrak{sl}_4,\mathrm{SO}(4))$-module $(\mathcal M_w)_{K_4}$ is irreducible for every even $w\ge6$. Its compact types are $$ \bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathcal Y_{w-2+2j}\simeq \bigoplus_{j\ge0}V_{w-2+2j}\boxtimes V_{w-2+2j}. $$ :::proof Proof of EI4 For a symmetric trace-free real matrix $A$, write $$ Q_A(x)=xAx^t,\quad D_AH=(xA)\cdot\nabla H, \quad T_AH=\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\partial_i\partial_jH. $$ Represent a compact type $H\in\mathcal Y_l$ by $f_H(x)=|x|^{-w-l}H(x)$. On $S^3$ the infinitesimal action is $$ dR(A)H=D_AH-(w+l)Q_AH. \tag{E13} $$ It has harmonic degrees $l+2,l,l-2$. Its projection onto degree $l-2$ is exactly $$ \operatorname{pr}_{l-2}dR(A)H =\frac{l+2-w}{4l(l+1)}T_AH. \tag{E14} $$ To see this, $\Delta D_AH=2T_AH$ and $\Delta^2(Q_AH)=8T_AH$. Harmonic decomposition therefore gives degree-$l-2$ terms $T_AH/(2l)$ in $D_AH|_{S^3}$ and $T_AH/[4l(l+1)]$ in $(Q_AH)|_{S^3}$, yielding (E14). The degree-$l+2$ term is $-(w+l)$ times the top harmonic part of $Q_AH$. The lowering map vanishes precisely at $l=w-2$ and is nonzero at every subsequent degree in (E12); the raising map is nonzero at every degree. Nonzeroness can be seen over the complexified Lie algebra by taking $H=(x_1+ix_2)^l$ and quadratic forms $(x_1\pm ix_2)^2$: the plus choice raises harmonically, the minus choice gives a nonzero $T_AH$ when $l\ge2$. Each $\mathcal Y_l$ is an irreducible $K_4$-module of multiplicity one. Any nonzero submodule contains a compact type; successive nonzero lowering and raising maps then give all of (E12). This proves irreducibility. The identification $\mathcal Y_l\simeq V_l\boxtimes V_l$ follows from the usual $\operatorname{Spin}(4)$ harmonic-polynomial representation; $(-1,-1)$ acts trivially. ::: :::: ## Nonvanishing and the automorphic realization ::::theorem EI5 | The coefficient-generated automorphic module Version: 1 Uses: [EI1](#ei1), [EI2](#ei2), [EI4](#ei4). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For odd $r\ge3$, the scalar components of $g\mapsto E_\nu(\mathbb Z^4g)$, $|\nu|=r$, generate an automorphic $(\mathfrak{sl}_4,\mathrm{SO}(4))$-module isomorphic to $(\mathcal M_{r+3})_{K_4}$. The Eisenstein map is injective on this module. Its minimal compact type is $\mathcal Y_{r+1}$. :::proof Proof of EI5 An intertwining sum could conceivably vanish on the entire module, so this needs a proof. Choose $H\in\mathcal Y_{w-2}$ with $H(e_4)\ne0$, and put $$ g_a=\operatorname{diag}(a,a,a,a^{-3}),\quad a\to\infty, \qquad f_H(x)=|x|^{-2w+2}H(x). $$ The rows $(0,0,0,k)$ contribute exactly $2\zeta(w)a^{3w}H(e_4)$. All other rows satisfy $|f_H(x)|\le C|x|^{-w}$. For $m'\ne0$, $$ \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(a^2|m'|^2+a^{-6}k^2)^{-w/2} \ll a^{-w}|m'|^{-w}+a^{4-w}|m'|^{1-w}. $$ Both sums over $m'\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus0$ converge for $w>4$. Consequently $$ \mathcal E_{f_H}(g_a)=2\zeta(w)a^{3w}H(e_4)+O(a^{4-w}). \tag{E15} $$ The Eisenstein map is nonzero on the minimal type, hence injective on the irreducible module (E12). The scalar components of the order-$r$ kernel derivatives contain a nonzero element of that type: for example $\partial_x^rG(ix)=-i(-1)^r(3)_r x^{-r-3}$ for $x>0$. Its compact orbit spans the type and its enveloping-algebra orbit spans (E12). ::: :::: :::discussion The fixed-order coefficients occupy the minimal compact type. General $\mathrm{SL}_4$ transformations generate the larger space (E12); they do not preserve the flat Fueter equation or act within the finite tuple of coefficients. This specifies an irreducible real-place Harish-Chandra module. It does not assert a unitary $L^2(\Gamma\backslash G_4)$ realization or a discrete series of $\mathrm{SL}_4$. The proof concerns the algebraic module of $K$-finite automorphic functions; a choice of globalization/topology or an adelic classification with finite-place constituents is additional work. A coefficient can vanish at a particular symmetric lattice even though the automorphic function is nonzero. For example cubic-lattice symmetries force numerous components to vanish. ::: ::::corollary EI6 | The first nonzero derivative order Version: 1 Uses: [EI3](#ei3), [EI5](#ei5). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $r=3$, the inducing degree is $-6$, the normalized character is $|d|^{-4}$, the minimal compact type is $V_4\boxtimes V_4$ of dimension $25$, and the finite-dimensional quotient of $I_6$ is $\mathcal P_2^\vee$ of dimension $10$. :::proof Proof of EI6 Insert $w=6$ in EI3–EI5. The dimensions are $(4+1)^2=25$ and $\binom{2+4-1}{3}=10$. ::: :::: ## Rotation covariance of the coefficient tuple ::::proposition EI7 | The coefficient action descends to the rotation group Version: 1 Uses: [Convergent sums](directions.md#n2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- Let $U_{-r-3}$ be the right-$\mathbb H$ span of the order-$r$ kernel derivatives, with $r>1$, and let $\rho(a,b)f(q)=bf(a^{-1}qb)$ for unit quaternions $a,b$. Set $\alpha_L(f)=\sum_{\lambda\ne0}f(\lambda)$. Then $$ (\sigma(a,b)\alpha)(f)=b\alpha(\rho(a,b)^{-1}f),\qquad \alpha_{aLb^{-1}}=\sigma(a,b)\alpha_L. $$ This is a genuine real representation on right-$\mathbb H$-linear functionals and factors through $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. :::proof Proof of EI7 The identity $G(a^{-1}qb)=b^{-1}G(q)a$ follows directly from the kernel formula. Differentiate it in any real coordinate directions. The chain rule expresses rotated order-$r$ derivatives using all four real derivative directions, with constant right quaternion factors. The kernel is also right regular: direct differentiation gives $\partial_tG+\partial_xG\,i+\partial_yG\,j+\partial_zG\,k=0$. This identity, and its derivatives, eliminate every time derivative in favor of spatial derivatives with right coefficients. Thus $U_{-r-3}$ is invariant under $\rho$. The formula for $\rho$ gives its group law and right-$\mathbb H$ linearity. Reindexing the absolutely convergent sum gives the displayed identity. For composition, the two output factors multiply as $b_1b_2$, and the precomposition is $\rho(k_2^{-1})\rho(k_1^{-1})=\rho((k_1k_2)^{-1})$. At $(-1,-1)$, the input representation is $-1$, while the output also gets $-1$, so $\sigma(-1,-1)\alpha(f)=-\alpha(-f)=\alpha(f)$. The kernel of $\operatorname{Spin}(4)\to\mathrm{SO}(4)$ therefore acts trivially. ::: :::: :::discussion The arithmetic quotient is $\Gamma\backslash G_4/K_4$; lattice stabilizers give the usual orbifold interpretation. The scalar-component model above avoids choosing local frames. The underlying induced representations are part of the theory studied by [[4]](#ref-gourevitch-2017); the proofs here specify our conventions directly. For the standard primitive-vector identity compare [[7]](#ref-sands-2022), §2.5. The following sections give the theta and special-value interpretation, including the cubic example. ::: :::discussion The coefficients of quaternionic elliptic functions can be converted into Mellin transforms of harmonic theta series. On the cubic lattice this leads to a specific newform and an exact, nonzero special value. The normalizations below distinguish the general even-lattice convention from the cubic example. ::: ## Harmonic theta series and Mellin integration Let $L\subset\mathbb R^4$ be a full Euclidean lattice, $H$ a scalar homogeneous harmonic polynomial of even degree $\ell>0$, and $N(x)=|x|^2$. In this article, $L^*$ denotes the Euclidean dual lattice. For an even integral lattice put $Q=N/2$ and $D=L^*/L$. In this case $\mu$ ranges over $D$, and $L+\mu$ denotes the corresponding coset in $L^*$. ::::definition TH-D1 | Harmonic Theta Functions Version: 1 Uses: [Harmonic numerators](#ei1). --- The **harmonic theta function** is $$ \theta_{L,H}(it)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}H(\lambda)e^{-\pi tN(\lambda)}\quad(t>0). $$ If the Euclidean bilinear form is integral on $L$ and $N(\lambda)$ is even for every $\lambda\in L$, the **coset theta functions** are $$ \Theta_\mu(\tau)=\sum_{\lambda\in L+\mu}H(\lambda)e^{2\pi i\tau Q(\lambda)},\quad \Theta_{L,H}=\Theta_0,\quad \operatorname{Im}\tau>0. $$ :::: Since $Q$ is integral on $L$, the zero component has integral exponents; for $\Theta_{L,H}=\sum_{m\ge1}a_me^{2\pi im\tau}$ put $L(\Theta_{L,H},s)=\sum_{m\ge1}a_mm^{-s}$ wherever absolutely convergent. ::::theorem TH1 | A convergent Mellin formula for each elliptic coefficient Version: 1 Uses: [TH-D1](#th-d1), [EI1](#ei1), [N2](directions.md#n2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- Let $\nu\in\mathbb N_0^3$ have odd order $r\ge3$, and let $H$ be any real component of the numerator $H_\nu$. For every full Euclidean lattice $L$, $$ E_{\nu,H}(L):=\sum_{\lambda\ne0}\frac{H(\lambda)}{N(\lambda)^{r+2}} =\frac{\pi^{r+2}}{\Gamma(r+2)}\int_0^\infty t^{r+1}\theta_{L,H}(it)\,dt. $$ Both the lattice sum and the interchange of summation and integration are absolutely convergent. :::proof Proof of TH1 The numerator has degree $r+1$. Thus each absolute summand is bounded by a constant times $|\lambda|^{-r-3}$, whose exponent exceeds the lattice dimension four. The gamma integral gives, for $s=r+2$, $$ \sum_{\lambda\ne0}|H(\lambda)|\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-\pi tN(\lambda)}dt =\frac{\Gamma(s)}{\pi^s}\sum_{\lambda\ne0}\frac{|H(\lambda)|}{N(\lambda)^s}<\infty. $$ Fubini's theorem now gives the formula. The argument also applies to any homogeneous harmonic numerator of degree $r+1$, including linear combinations of the kernel numerators. ::: :::: ::::corollary TH3 | Critical values with all normalizing factors fixed Version: 1 Uses: [TH1](#th1), [TH2](harmonic-theta-modularity.md#th2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- Under TH1's hypotheses, if $L$ is even integral, then $$ E_{\nu,H}(L)=2^{-(r+2)}L(\Theta_{L,H},r+2). $$ The theta form has weight $k=r+3$, and the evaluation point is $k-1$. In particular the first potentially nonzero coefficients, of order $r=3$, evaluate weight-six cusp forms at $s=5$. :::proof Proof of TH3 Group the absolutely convergent lattice sum by $m=Q(\lambda)$ and use $N(\lambda)=2m$. This gives exactly the factor $2^{-(r+2)}$. TH2 gives the weight. The usual critical integers for the weight-$k$ holomorphic cusp-form $L$-function are $1,\ldots,k-1$, from the archimedean gamma factors in the functional equation; hence this is the upper critical value in the classical normalization. No Hecke-eigenform hypothesis is required for the identity. ::: :::: ## The cubic lattice and a weight-six newform Let $L_0=\mathbb Z+\mathbb Zi+\mathbb Zj+\mathbb Zk$ and put $$ H_4(t,x,y,z)=t^4+x^4+y^4+z^4-\frac12(t^2+x^2+y^2+z^2)^2. $$ In this example the Fourier exponent uses $Q_0(m)=|m|^2$, rather than $N/2$: $$ \vartheta(\tau)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^4}H_4(m)e^{2\pi i\tau|m|^2},\qquad f(\tau)=\eta(2\tau)^{12}. $$ Here $u=e^{2\pi i\tau}$ and $\eta(\tau)=u^{1/24}\prod_{n\ge1}(1-u^n)$. Expanding the product gives $$ f(\tau)=u\prod_{n\ge1}(1-u^{2n})^{12} =u-12u^3+54u^5-88u^7-99u^9+\cdots. $$ For this Fourier convention $L(f,s)=\sum_{m\ge1}a_mm^{-s}$ when $f=\sum a_mu^m$. ::::theorem TH4 | The exact harmonic theta identity Version: 1 Uses: [TH2](harmonic-theta-modularity.md#th2), [TH-D2](#th-d2), the scalar theta, eta-quotient, and modular-form dimension theorems cited below. Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- One has $$ \vartheta(\tau)=4\eta(2\tau)^{12},\qquad \sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^4\setminus\{0\}}\frac{H_4(m)}{|m|^{10}}=4L(f,5). $$ The normalized eta product $f$ is the unique newform in $S_6(\Gamma_0(4))$, with trivial character. :::proof Proof of TH4 First $\Delta\sum x_j^4=12N$ and $\Delta(N^2)=24N$, so $H_4$ is harmonic. To use TH2 without changing the Fourier convention, take the even Euclidean lattice $\sqrt2L_0$, of Gram matrix $2I_4$. Its theta series with numerator $H_4$ is $4\vartheta$, because $H_4(\sqrt2m)=4H_4(m)$. Its level is four, its determinant is sixteen, and the scalar theta transformation theorem [[8, Thm. 4]](#ref-simard-2015) gives weight $2+4=6$ and character $\big(16/\cdot\big)=1$ on $\Gamma_0(4)$. Hence $\vartheta\in S_6(\Gamma_0(4))$. For the eta product use the eta-quotient criterion and cusp-order formula [[1, Thms. 2.4–2.5]](#ref-eta-quotients-2018). For $\prod_{\delta\mid N}\eta(\delta\tau)^{r_\delta}$ the weight is $\tfrac12\sum r_\delta$, the congruences are $\sum\delta r_\delta\equiv\sum(N/\delta)r_\delta\equiv0\pmod{24}$, and the character is the Kronecker symbol associated to $(-1)^k\prod\delta^{r_\delta}$. Here $N=4$, $r_2=12$, and both sums equal $24$. The character is trivial since $2^{12}$ is a square. At a cusp of denominator $c\mid4$ the order is $$ \frac4{24}\sum_{\delta\mid4} \frac{\gcd(c,\delta)^2r_\delta}{\gcd(c,4/c)c\delta}=1 \quad(c=1,2,4). $$ Thus $f$ is a nonzero cusp form of the same weight, level, and character. The dimension formula [[3, Thm. 3.5.1]](#ref-diamond-shurman-2005), for even $k>2$, is $$ \dim S_k(\Gamma)=(k-1)(g-1)+(k/2-1)c +\lfloor k/4\rfloor e_2+\lfloor k/3\rfloor e_3. $$ For $\Gamma_0(4)$ the index is six, there are three cusps, no elliptic points, and genus zero. The formula gives $-5+2\cdot3=1$. For level one the data $(g,c,e_2,e_3)=(0,1,1,1)$ give dimension zero in weight six; for level two the data $(0,2,1,0)$ also give zero. Therefore there is no oldspace at level four. The eight shortest lattice vectors have $H_4=1/2$, so the first coefficient of $\vartheta$ is four. The first coefficient of $f$ is one. Equality follows from the one-dimensional cusp space. Its normalized generator is a Hecke eigenform and is new because the oldspace is zero. Finally group the absolutely convergent harmonic lattice sum by $|m|^2$ to obtain $L(\vartheta,5)=4L(f,5)$; TH1's convergence estimate applies to any harmonic quartic. ::: :::: ::::theorem TH5 | An individual quaternionic elliptic coefficient Version: 1 Uses: [TH4](#th4), [N1](directions.md#n1), [N2](directions.md#n2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- With $G(q)=\bar q/|q|^4$, spatial derivative $\partial_x$ in the $i$ direction, and the cubic lattice $L_0$, $$ E_{(3,0,0)}(L_0)=\sum_{\lambda\ne0}\partial_x^3G(\lambda) =192\,i\,L\!\left(\eta(2\tau)^{12},5\right)\ne0. $$ For the elliptic function $\wp_{L_0,1}$ of [E-C1](elliptic-functions.md#e-c1), the coefficient of $x^2$ in the real Taylor expansion of its regular part $\wp_{L_0,1}-G_1$ at zero is $96iL(f,5)$. :::proof Proof of TH5 Differentiate the $i$ component $-x/N^2$ of $G$ three times. It gives $$ \frac{12N^2-144x^2N+192x^4}{N^5}. $$ The real, $j$, and $k$ components have a coordinate of odd parity and vanish after summation over the sign-symmetric lattice. Absolute convergence justifies these cancellations and coordinate permutations. Average the displayed numerator over the four coordinate positions; its lattice sum is unchanged, while its value becomes $$ 12N^2-36N^2+48(t^4+x^4+y^4+z^4)=48H_4. $$ TH4 therefore gives $E_{(3,0,0)}=48i\cdot4L(f,5)$. The Mellin identity $$ L(f,5)=\frac{(2\pi)^5}{\Gamma(5)}\int_0^\infty f(it)t^4dt $$ follows by the same absolute integration argument as TH1 (the harmonic coefficient sum converges at five). Every factor of $\eta(2it)^{12}$ is positive for $t>0$, so this value is strictly positive. Finally N1 with $\mu=(2,0,0)$ gives the second derivative of the regular part. Division by $2!$ gives its ordinary Taylor coefficient. ::: :::: ## How the representations fit together :::discussion | Object varied | Group | Result established here | | --- | --- | --- | | A regular function on the ball, with its point moved by Möbius transformations | $\mathrm{Sp}(1,1)$ | [Discrete series](fueter-discrete-series.md) for compatible spinors; the [Hardy limit](fueter-hardy-space.md) for one quaternionic value. | | The lattice in a kernel-derivative sum | $\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb R)$ | An [irreducible module of Eisenstein functions](#ei5). | | The modular variable of the cubic harmonic theta form | $\mathrm{GL}_2$, or the classical modular group | TH4–TH6 identify a weight-six newform and its critical value. | The theta and Mellin formulas provide the stated numerical bridge. An equivalence or functorial correspondence between the first two representations has not been established. An arbitrary lattice theta form need not be an eigenform and may vanish; the cubic example succeeds because its cusp space has dimension one. Its newform data also agree with [[5, 4.6.a]](#ref-lmfdb-46a). ::: ## Questions opened by the example :::discussion Which other arithmetic lattices and individual quaternionic coefficients select a single newform? Can lattice symmetries predict vanishing or isolate Hecke constituents? What algebraic periods normalize the resulting critical values, and how do these values interact with quaternionic multiplication? These questions remain open here. At derivative order $r=1$, the predicted theta weight is four and the evaluation point is three. TH1 does not apply: the original lattice sum is at the boundary of absolute convergence. Cuspidality still makes the theta Mellin integral meaningful on an even integral lattice, but comparison with a specified regularization or with elliptic quasi-periods needs a separate proof. ::: ## Related Results [Modularity and cuspidality of the coset vector](harmonic-theta-modularity.md#th2). [The modular representation attached to the example](harmonic-theta-modularity.md#th6). ## References 1. --- title: From lattice sums to number theory description: Eisenstein sums and coefficient identities, separated from open research directions. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: exposition order: 3 --- # From lattice sums to number theory :::discussion The elliptic construction starts from an arbitrary full-rank lattice. Its coefficients supply a first connection to lattice Eisenstein sums. The precise statements below lead to representations and special values, followed by questions about arithmetic multiplication and periods. ::: ## Higher derivatives and Eisenstein sums For $\nu=(n_1,n_2,n_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, set $$ |\nu|=n_1+n_2+n_3,\quad \partial^\nu=\partial_{x_1}^{n_1}\partial_{x_2}^{n_2}\partial_{x_3}^{n_3}, \quad G_\nu=\partial^\nu G. $$ Write $\epsilon_j$ for the multi-index with a single $1$ in position $j$, for $j\in\{1,2,3\}$. ::::construction N-C1 | Higher Eisenstein and elliptic sums Version: 1 Uses: [N-D1](#n-d1), [lattice setup](elliptic-functions.md#e-d1). Justification: Absolute convergence and periodicity in [N2](#n2). Origin: consequence --- Let $L\subset\mathbb H$ be a full-rank lattice and let $\nu\in\mathbb N_0^3$ satisfy $|\nu|\ge2$. Form $$ E_\nu(L)=\sum_{\lambda\in L^*}G_\nu(\lambda), \qquad \wp_{L,\nu}(q)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}G_\nu(q+\lambda)-E_\nu(L) \quad(q\notin L). $$ :::: ::::proposition N2 | Convergence and periodicity of the higher sums Version: 1 Uses: [N-C1](#n-c1), [F2](foundations.md#f2), the lattice-count estimate in [E1](elliptic-functions.md#e1). Review: pending Formal: verified Formal-evidence: [Lean checking record](../evidence/lean-N1-v2.html#MathResearch.Fueter.N2_v1) Origin: consequence --- For every full-rank lattice $L\subset\mathbb H$ and every $\nu\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\nu|\ge2$, the Eisenstein series in N-C1 converges absolutely. The defining series for $\wp_{L,\nu}$ converges absolutely and locally uniformly on $\mathbb H\setminus L$. For every $\omega\in L$ and $q\notin L$, $$ \wp_{L,\nu}(q+\omega)=\wp_{L,\nu}(q). $$ :::proof Proof of N2 F2 gives decay $|q|^{-3-|\nu|}$, with exponent at least $5$. The lattice-count estimate from the proof of E1 therefore proves absolute convergence, uniformly on compact sets away from the lattice for the translated sum. Absolute convergence permits reindexing $\lambda\mapsto\lambda+\omega$, which proves periodicity. ::: :::: ::::proposition N1 | Coefficients at the singularity Version: 2 Uses: [N-D1](#n-d1), [N-C1](#n-c1), [N2](#n2), [E1](elliptic-functions.md#e1). Review: pending Formal: verified Formal-evidence: [Lean checking record](../evidence/lean-N1-v2.html#MathResearch.Fueter.N1_v2) Origin: consequence --- Let $L\subset\mathbb H$ be a full-rank lattice and $j\in\{1,2,3\}$. Let $h_j$ be the smooth extension near $0$ of $\wp_{L,j}-G_j$ supplied by E1. For every $\mu\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\mu|\ge1$, $$ \partial^\mu h_j(0)=E_{\mu+\epsilon_j}(L). $$ :::proof Proof of N1 Differentiate the convergent series for $h_j$ from E1 and evaluate at $q=0$. The subtracted constants disappear, leaving $\sum_{\lambda\in L^*}G_{\mu+\epsilon_j}(\lambda)$. This converges absolutely since $|\mu+\epsilon_j|\ge2$. ::: :::: ::::corollary N3 | Parity cancellation Version: 1 Uses: [N-C1](#n-c1), [N2](#n2), [F2](foundations.md#f2). Review: pending Formal: verified Formal-evidence: [Lean checking record](../evidence/lean-N1-v2.html#MathResearch.Fueter.N3_v1) Origin: derivation --- For every full-rank lattice $L\subset\mathbb H$ and every $\nu\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with even $|\nu|\ge2$, $$ E_\nu(L)=0. $$ :::proof Proof of N3 By F2, $G_\nu$ is odd when $|\nu|$ is even. The terms at $\lambda$ and $-\lambda$ cancel, and absolute convergence from N2 justifies pairing them. ::: :::: :::discussion These are foundational identities, with no novelty claim. They explain how higher Eisenstein sums enter the regular part of the elliptic construction. Among the absolutely convergent sums, order $2$ vanishes by N3, so order $3$ is the first order not eliminated by this parity argument. For related lattice sums and Laurent coefficients, see [[1]](#ref-krausshar-2001), §§4–5. ::: ## Eisenstein representations :::discussion Varying the lattice produces [Eisenstein functions on SL₄](lattice-eisenstein-series.md). Their irreducible module, inducing parameter, and compact types are established there with proofs. This lattice action differs from the Möbius action on regular functions in [the discrete-series](fueter-discrete-series.md) and [Hardy](fueter-hardy-space.md) constructions. ::: ## Harmonic theta series :::discussion The kernel derivatives have [harmonic polynomial numerators](lattice-eisenstein-series.md#ei1). Their convergent lattice sums admit a [Mellin formula](lattice-eisenstein-series.md#th1); even integral lattices give [harmonic theta cusp forms](harmonic-theta-modularity.md#th2) and [critical L-values](lattice-eisenstein-series.md#th3). The [cubic example](lattice-eisenstein-series.md#th5) identifies a specific coefficient with the value at five of the weight-six newform η(2τ)¹². The order-one sum and its proposed connection to quasi-periods still need a regularization theorem. Other arithmetic lattices, Hecke decompositions, and algebraic period normalizations remain open directions. ::: :::discussion Open directions — no theorem asserted ## Multiplication and arithmetic lattices Lattices with an action by elements of a quaternion algebra suggest transformation laws for the elliptic functions and quasi-periods. The action and its hypotheses need precise statements. A transformation identity and an independent arithmetic constraint are different conclusions. ## Period relations The additivity of $\eta_L$ is part of [E3](elliptic-functions.md#e3). Relating it to a residue or to integrals on $\mathbb H/L$ requires further statements fixing normalization, orientation, and left/right regularity. The [closed pairings and pullback identities](regular-differential-forms.md) supply local results; quotient cohomology remains open. The [literature guide](literature.md) collects sources and further reading. These questions remain in the research notebook for investigation. ::: The full-lattice Eisenstein sum in N-C1 is twice the positive-semilattice sum of [[1, §4, eq. (8), p. 1018]](#ref-krausshar-2001) at odd derivative order. The regularized first-derivative sum is [[1, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019]](#ref-krausshar-2001). N1 uses real Taylor derivatives; the source’s expansion [[1, eq. (13), p. 1020]](#ref-krausshar-2001) uses Fueter polynomials. ## References 1. R. S. Kraußhar, [*On a New Type of Eisenstein Series in Clifford Analysis*](https://doi.org/10.4171/ZAA/1057), Zeitschrift für Analysis und ihre Anwendungen **20** (2001), no. 4, 1007–1029. [Open text](https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/35214).

--- title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity description: Definitions of Fueter regularity and the kernel, with explicit statements and proofs. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: exposition order: 1 --- # Quaternions and Fueter regularity :::discussion The Cauchy–Fueter kernel is the starting point for the elliptic construction. This page fixes the conventions and collects the elementary facts needed later. Prerequisites are real multivariable calculus and quaternion multiplication. ::: ## Quaternions and coordinates Let $\mathbb H$ be the real quaternion algebra with basis $(1,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,i,j,k)$ and multiplication $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$. Write $$ q=t+e_1x_1+e_2x_2+e_3x_3,\qquad x_0=t,\quad e_0=1. $$ For $q=t+e_1x_1+e_2x_2+e_3x_3$, write its quaternionic conjugate and Euclidean norm as $$ \bar q=t-e_1x_1-e_2x_2-e_3x_3,\qquad |q|=(t^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)^{1/2}. $$ The multiplication relations give $q\bar q=\bar q q=|q|^2$, since the mixed imaginary terms cancel in pairs. All partial derivatives below are ordinary real derivatives in these fixed coordinates. ## The regularity equation For an open set $U\subset\mathbb H$ and a smooth function $f:U\to\mathbb H$, define $$ D_\ell f=\partial_t f+\sum_{j=1}^3e_j\partial_{x_j}f, \qquad D_r f=\partial_t f+\sum_{j=1}^3(\partial_{x_j}f)e_j. $$ ::::definition F-D2 | Left and Right Fueter Regularity Version: 1 Uses: [quaternion conjugation and norm](#f-d1), [Fueter operators](#fueter-operators). --- A smooth function $f:U\to\mathbb H$ on an open set $U\subset\mathbb H$ is **left Fueter-regular** if $D_\ell f=0$, and **right Fueter-regular** if $D_r f=0$ on $U$. :::: “Regular” in these articles refers to Fueter regularity, with the side specified when needed. :::discussion Multiplying either operator by a nonzero real scalar does not change its kernel. The side on which a quaternionic coefficient acts matters. ::: :::example Products need not preserve left regularity The constant $i$ and $z_2=tj-x_2$ are left regular, since $D_\ell i=0$ and $D_\ell z_2=j-j=0$. But $$ D_\ell(i z_2)=ij-ji=2k\ne0. $$ Thus pointwise multiplication does not preserve left regularity. ::: ## The Cauchy–Fueter kernel ::::definition F-D3 | The Cauchy–Fueter Kernel Version: 1 Uses: [quaternion conjugation and norm](#f-d1). --- The **Cauchy–Fueter kernel** is the function $$ G:\mathbb H\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathbb H,\qquad G(q)=\frac{\bar q}{|q|^4}. $$ :::: Write $G_j=\partial_{x_j}G$ for $j=1,2,3$. There is no surface-area factor in this normalization. ::::proposition F1 | Regularity of the kernel Version: 2 Uses: [F-D2](#f-d2), [F-D3](#f-d3); the kernel identity [[1, §4, Lemma 2]](#ref-sudbery-1979). Review: pending Formal: verified Formal-evidence: [Lean build and axiom audit](../evidence/lean-F1-v2.html#MathResearch.Fueter.F1_v2) Origin: consequence --- The kernel $G$ of F-D3 is both left and right Fueter-regular on $\mathbb H\setminus\{0\}$. For every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^4$, its real partial derivative $\partial^\alpha G$ is also both left and right regular there. :::proof Proof of F1 Put $x_0=t$ and $e_0=1$, so $q=\sum_{\mu=0}^3e_\mu x_\mu$. Since $D_\ell\bar q=4$ and $\partial_{x_\mu}|q|^{-4}=-4x_\mu|q|^{-6}$, the product rule gives $$ D_\ell G =4|q|^{-4}-4|q|^{-6}\sum_{\mu=0}^3 e_\mu\bar q\,x_\mu =4|q|^{-4}-4|q|^{-6}q\bar q=0. $$ For $D_r$, the sum in the second term is instead $\sum_\mu\bar q\,e_\mu x_\mu=\bar q q$, with the same result. Real partial derivatives commute with both constant-coefficient operators, which proves the final assertion. ::: :::: ## Derivatives and decay ::::lemma F2 | Parity, homogeneity, and derivative bounds Version: 1 Uses: [quaternion conjugation and norm](#f-d1), [F-D3](#f-d3). Review: pending Formal: verified Formal-evidence: [Lean build and axiom audit](../evidence/lean-F2-v1.html#MathResearch.Fueter.F2_v1) Origin: derivation --- For every $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^4$, there is a constant $C_\alpha$ such that, for all $q\ne0$ and all real $a>0$, $$ \begin{aligned} \partial^\alpha G(aq)&=a^{-3-|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha G(q),\\ \partial^\alpha G(-q)&=(-1)^{|\alpha|+1}\partial^\alpha G(q),\\ |\partial^\alpha G(q)|&\le C_\alpha |q|^{-3-|\alpha|}. \end{aligned} $$ In particular, $G$ is odd, each $G_j$ is even, and $$ G_j(q)=-\frac{e_j}{|q|^4}-\frac{4x_j\bar q}{|q|^6}. $$ :::proof Proof of F2 The defining formula gives $G(aq)=a^{-3}G(q)$ and $G(-q)=-G(q)$. Differentiating these identities in the real coordinates proves the homogeneity and parity formulas. The smooth function $\partial^\alpha G$ is bounded on the compact unit sphere. Write $q=|q|u$ with $|u|=1$ and apply homogeneity to obtain the bound. Finally, the formula for $G_j$ follows from $\partial_{x_j}\bar q=-e_j$ and $\partial_{x_j}|q|^{-4}=-4x_j|q|^{-6}$. ::: :::: :::discussion A four-dimensional lattice sum with decay $|\lambda|^{-p}$ converges absolutely for $p>4$, as shown in [E1](elliptic-functions.md#e1). The first derivatives $G_j$ are at the borderline $p=4$. The elliptic construction gains another power of decay by subtracting a constant term. ::: :::discussion Sources and next reading Fueter's foundational papers and Sudbery's exposition are listed in the [literature guide](literature.md#foundations-and-periodic-functions). The conventions used here are given with [conjugation and norm](#f-d1), [regularity](#f-d2) and [the kernel](#f-d3); the arguments above establish the displayed identities in those conventions. Continue to [Quaternionic elliptic functions](elliptic-functions.md). ::: ## Further constructions :::discussion On the ball, the regular equation has [weighted symmetric-spinor realizations of discrete series](fueter-discrete-series.md) and a [Hardy-space realization of a limit of discrete series](fueter-hardy-space.md). For differential geometry, [mixed left/right pairings](regular-differential-forms.md#df1) produce closed three-forms. These articles use the conventions fixed here. ::: ## References 1. A. Sudbery, [*Quaternionic analysis*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100055638), Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society **85** (1979), no. 2, 199–225.
